claim: Zebrafish klc4 has two alternative splice isoforms, one long and one short.
source: In zebrafish, the long klc4 transcript encodes a full length protein of 620 amino acids while the short isoform is predicted to encode a 185 amino acid protein, ending just before the LFP motif (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the two isoforms based on their predicted protein lengths and structural features.

claim: Both klc4 isoforms are expressed throughout early zebrafish development.
source: We found that both isoforms are expressed throughout early development, with expression detectable at 2 hours post fertilization (hpf) and continuing through the initial period of neuronal axon outgrowth, pathfinding and branching, between 16 and 28 hpf (Figure 1B).
evidence: RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B demonstrates expression of both isoforms at multiple developmental timepoints.

claim: At 24 hpf, klc4 is expressed in clusters of neurons in the telencephalon, epiphysis, diencephalon, ventral midbrain and hindbrain, and in the trigeminal and the posterior lateral line (pLL) ganglia.
source: At 24 hpf, klc4 is expressed in clusters of neurons in the telencephalon, epiphysis, diencephalon, ventral midbrain and hindbrain, and in the trigeminal and the posterior lateral line (pLL) ganglia (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C and D demonstrates spatial expression pattern.

claim: In the spinal cord, klc4 is strongly expressed in the Rohon-Beard sensory neurons, and at lower levels in other neuron populations.
source: In the spinal cord, klc4 is strongly expressed in the Rohon-Beard sensory neurons, and at lower levels in other neuron populations (Figure 1E).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1E demonstrates expression levels in different spinal cord neuron populations.

claim: At 48 hpf, klc4 continues to be expressed broadly in the nervous system with high expression levels in the trigeminal ganglia, pLL ganglia, and RB neurons.
source: At 48 hpf, klc4 continues to be expressed broadly in the nervous system with high expression levels in the trigeminal ganglia, pLL ganglia, and RB neurons (Figure 1F, G and H).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1F, G and H demonstrates continued expression at 48 hpf.

claim: The full-length klc4 mRNA is present in developing neurons.
source: A riboprobe that only binds the long isoform shows a similar expression pattern to the probe that recognizes both isoforms (Figure 1I, J and K), indicating the full-length klc4 mRNA is present in developing neurons.
evidence: In situ hybridization with long isoform-specific probe shows similar pattern to pan-isoform probe.

claim: The klc4uw314 allele has a 25 bp deletion in exon 3 from 404bp to 428bp in the heptad repeat region that leads to an early stop after 9 missense amino acids.
source: One resulting allele, klc4uw314, has a 25 bp deletion in exon 3 from 404bp to 428bp in the heptad repeat region that leads to an early stop after 9 missense amino acids (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the specific mutation generated by CRISPR/Cas9 and its predicted effect on the protein.

claim: Homozygous klc4uw314 mutant embryos show virtually no klc4 mRNA expression.
source: In situ hybridization analysis of homozygous klc4uw314 mutant embryos showed virtually no klc4 mRNA expression, suggesting that the mutant transcript undergoes nonsense-mediated decay (Figure 1L, M and N).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1L, M and N demonstrates absence of klc4 mRNA in mutants.

claim: The mutant klc4uw314 transcript undergoes nonsense-mediated decay.
source: In situ hybridization analysis of homozygous klc4uw314 mutant embryos showed virtually no klc4 mRNA expression, suggesting that the mutant transcript undergoes nonsense-mediated decay (Figure 1L, M and N).
evidence: The absence of mRNA in mutants despite the presence of the gene suggests degradation by nonsense-mediated decay.

claim: RB peripheral axon branches appear less dense in klc4uw314 mutant embryos compared to wild type.
source: Inspection of mutant embryos revealed that RB peripheral axon branches appeared less dense and displayed less overall innervation of the sensory field compared to wild type (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Light sheet microscopy images shown in Figure 2A and B demonstrate reduced branch density in mutants.

claim: klc4uw314 mutant embryos have fewer peripheral axons at each region of interest compared to wild type.
source: Consistent with our visual impression of reduced branching, mutant embryos had consistently fewer axons at each ROI (Figure 2F).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 2F demonstrates statistically significant reduction in axon number across multiple ROIs.

claim: Treatment of wild type embryos with 100 µM Kinesore from 17 hpf to 24 hpf causes a reduction in axon branch number in ventral regions at 24 hpf.
source: We found that treatment of wild type embryos with 100 µM Kinesore during early stages of peripheral axon arborization, from 17 hpf to 24 hpf, caused a reduction in axon branch number in ventral regions at 24 hpf of a similar magnitude to that seen in klc4uw314 mutants (Figure 2G-I), although more dorsal branching appears unaffected.
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 2G-I demonstrates reduced branching in Kinesore-treated embryos.

claim: There is no difference in the rate of branch initiation between klc4uw314 mutant and wild-type embryos.
source: Surprisingly, we found no difference in the rate of branch initiation between klc4uw314 mutant and wild-type embryos (Figure 3C).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 3C shows no significant difference in branch initiation rates.

claim: In both wild type and klc4uw314 mutants, new branches are initiated via GCB more frequently than IB.
source: In both conditions, new branches were initiated via GCB more frequently than IB, but there was no difference in the proportion of GCB versus IB branching events between wild-type and klc4uw314 mutants.
evidence: The manuscript states that GCB is more frequent than IB in both conditions based on live imaging data.

claim: In klc4uw314 mutants, 57.7% of GCB branches and 61.9% of IB branches retract after initiating.
source: Quantification showed that in klc4uw314 mutants, 57.7% of GCB branches and 61.9% of IB branches retracted after initiating, compared to 14.2% of GCB and 11.8% of IB branches in wild type (Figure 3D).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 3D provides specific percentages of branch retraction.

claim: klc4uw314 mutant axons grow at a faster rate than wild type axons.
source: This phenotype cannot be explained as a general axon growth defect, as klc4uw314 mutant axons grew at a faster rate than wild type axons (Figure 3E).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 3E demonstrates significantly faster growth velocity in mutant axons.

claim: KLC4 is required for stabilization of axon branches.
source: Thus, these data suggest that KLC4 is required specifically for stabilization of axon branches.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation that branches initiate normally but retract more frequently in mutants.

claim: In wild-type embryos, most axons are oriented in ventral-posterior and ventral-anterior directions, with a higher proportion of axon signal in posteriorly directed angles.
source: In wild-type embryos, most axons are oriented in ventral-posterior and ventral-anterior directions, with a higher proportion of axon signal in posteriorly directed angles, peaking approximately between –50° and –85° (Figure 4A and C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Automated orientation analysis shown in Figure 4A and C demonstrates the directional distribution of axons.

claim: klc4uw314 mutants have reduced overall axon signal compared to wild-type.
source: In contrast, klc4uw314 mutants had reduced overall axon signal compared to their wild-type cousins (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), consistent with the reduced branch density.
evidence: Orientation analysis shown in Figure 4B and C demonstrates reduced total axon signal in mutants.

claim: klc4uw314 mutants show a small but significant increase in axons oriented in the posterior direction, specifically those oriented between –20.5° and –50.5°.
source: We found a small but significant increase in axons oriented in the posterior direction in klc4uw314 mutants, specifically those oriented between –20.5° and –50.5° (Figure 4D).
evidence: Normalized orientation analysis shown in Figure 4D demonstrates statistically significant increase in posterior-oriented axons.

claim: klc4uw314 mutant axons have a preference for posterior growth paths.
source: We found klc4uw314 mutant axons had a preference for posterior growth paths, while wild-type axons had no anterior-posterior bias (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Rose plots shown in Figure 5B and C demonstrate directional growth preferences.

claim: In wild-type embryos, as growth cones bifurcate, the sister branches grow away from each other, resulting in an average branch angle of 96.5 degrees 15 min after branch formation, and 91.7 degrees 75 min after branch formation.
source: As growth cones bifurcate in wild-type embryos, the sister branches grow away from each other (Figure 5D' and E, Figure 5—video 1), resulting in an average branch angle of 96.5 degrees 15 min after branch formation, and 91.7 degrees 75 min after branch formation (Figure 5E and G).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 5E and G provides specific measurements of sister branch angles over time.

claim: In klc4uw314 mutants, newly formed branches do not separate as much, resulting in a shallower average angle of 79.7 degrees between sister branches 15 min after branch formation, and narrowing to 60.2 degrees after 75 min.
source: In klc4uw314 mutants, the newly formed branches did not separate as much, resulting in a shallower average angle of 79.7 degrees between sister branches 15 min after branch formation, and narrowing to 60.2 degrees after 75 min (Figure 5F and G, Figure 5—video 2).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 5F and G provides specific measurements of sister branch angles in mutants.

claim: KLC4 may be involved in mediating mutual repulsion between sister axon branches.
source: These results suggest that KLC4 may be involved in mediating mutual repulsion between sister axon branches.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation that sister branches fail to separate properly in mutants.

claim: In wild type embryos, when a peripheral axon growth cone contacts another axon it retracts or changes direction to grow away from the other axon.
source: Live imaging also revealed a broader defect in axon repulsion: normally, in wild type embryos when a peripheral axon growth cone contacts another axon (either a branch of the same neuron or of another neuron) it retracts or changes direction to grow away from the other axon, thus minimizing contact between axons (Sagasti et al., 2005; Liu and Halloran, 2005; Figure 6A).
evidence: Live imaging data shown in Figure 6A demonstrates contact-mediated retraction in wild type, and the statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In klc4uw314 mutants, axons often fasciculate after contacts and grow together for substantial distances.
source: However, in klc4uw314 mutants, axons often fasciculate after such contacts and grow together for substantial distances (Figure 6B and C, Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: Live imaging data shown in Figure 6B and C demonstrates fasciculation behavior in mutants.

claim: In wild-type embryos, all observed fasciculations (n=3) resolved by retraction or defasciculation.
source: In wild-type embryos, all observed fasciculations (n=3) resolved by retraction or defasciculation, but only 46.5% of fasciculations (n=19) in klc4uw314 mutants were resolved in this manner.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of fasciculation resolution events.

claim: Fasciculation events are rare in wild type embryos but occur relatively frequently in klc4uw314 mutants.
source: We found that fasciculation events were rare in wild type embryos but occurred relatively frequently in mutants (Figure 6D).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 6D demonstrates significantly higher fasciculation frequency in mutants.

claim: KLC4 is important for the mutual repulsion needed to shape sensory arbors.
source: Together, these results show that KLC4 is important for the mutual repulsion needed to shape sensory arbors.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from observations of increased fasciculation and reduced repulsion in mutants.

claim: KLC4 may be involved in the localization of factors controlling central versus peripheral axon behavior.
source: The failure of klc4uw314 mutant peripheral axons to show repulsion suggests that KLC4 may be involved in the localization of factors controlling central versus peripheral axon behavior.
evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that peripheral axons in mutants behave like central axons (fasciculation instead of repulsion).

claim: Some RB neurons in klc4uw314 mutant embryos project a process from the apical cell body that crosses the midline within the dorsal spinal cord.
source: We found that some RB neurons in Tg(–3.1ngn1:gfp-caax);klc4uw314 mutant embryos and Kinesore-treated embryos projected a process from the apical cell body that crossed the midline within the dorsal spinal cord (Figure 7A and B, Figure 7—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Imaging data shown in Figure 7A and B demonstrates midline-crossing apical processes in mutants.

claim: 4% of neurons in klc4uw314 mutants have midline crossing processes compared to 1% in wild type embryos.
source: We counted the number of midline crossing apical processes from images of anti-HNK-1-labeled embryos captured in the spinal cord overlying the yolk extension and found that 4% of neurons (n=1,509 neurons in 51 embryos) in klc4uw314 mutants had midline crossing processes compared to 1% in wild type embryos (n=608 neurons in 21 embryos) (Figure 7C).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 7C provides specific percentages of neurons with midline-crossing processes.

claim: 7% of Kinesore-treated neurons have apical protrusions that cross the midline, compared to 2% of neurons in vehicle-treated control.
source: Similar results were obtained following treatment with Kinesore from 18 to 24 hpf, with 7% of Kinesore-treated neurons (n=433 neurons in 17 embryos) extending an apical protrusion that crossed the midline, compared to 2% of neurons in vehicle-treated control (n=436 neurons in 15 embryos) (Figure 7C).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 7C provides specific percentages for Kinesore-treated embryos.

claim: The apical processes in klc4uw314 mutants and kinesore-treated embryos fasciculate with the contralateral central axon fascicle.
source: This mosaic cell labeling showed that the apical processes grew to and fasciculated with the contralateral central axon fascicle in both klc4uw314 mutant and kinesore-treated embryos (Figure 7D and F), suggesting they may respond to cues directing central axon behavior despite emerging from an ectopic apical location.
evidence: Mosaic labeling shown in Figure 7D and F demonstrates fasciculation of apical processes with contralateral central axons.

claim: KLC4 may play a role in determining the location of axon emergence from the cell body.
source: These results suggest that KLCs have a role in determining the location of axon emergence from the cell body.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation of ectopic apical axons in mutants.

claim: In klc4uw314 mutants, a smaller proportion of Rab5 vesicles move in the anterograde direction compared to wild type.
source: In klc4uw314 mutants, a smaller proportion of vesicles moved in the anterograde direction compared to wild type (Figure 8B), and the maximum anterograde vesicle run length was reduced (Figure 8C), suggesting that some aspects of Rab5 vesicle transport or a subset of Rab5 vesicles rely on KLC4 function.
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 8B demonstrates reduced proportion of anterograde-moving vesicles in mutants.

claim: The maximum anterograde vesicle run length is reduced in klc4uw314 mutants.
source: In klc4uw314 mutants, a smaller proportion of vesicles moved in the anterograde direction compared to wild type (Figure 8B), and the maximum anterograde vesicle run length was reduced (Figure 8C), suggesting that some aspects of Rab5 vesicle transport or a subset of Rab5 vesicles rely on KLC4 function.
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 8C demonstrates reduced maximum run length in mutants.

claim: There is no significant difference in velocity of Rab5 vesicles that are moving between wild type and klc4uw314 mutants.
source: However, there was no significant difference in velocity of the Rab5 vesicles that were moving, suggesting these vesicles can attach to the motor without KLC4 (Figure 8D).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 8D shows no significant difference in vesicle velocity.

claim: KLC4 does not play a significant role in vesicle delivery from the cell body to branch points.
source: In both wild type and klc4 mutant neurons, the intensity increased similarly during this period, suggesting KLC4 does not play a significant role in vesicle delivery from the cell body to branch points (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Photoactivation experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B show similar accumulation of Rab5 at branch points in wild type and mutants.

claim: There is no change in the percentage of retrograde EB3-GFP comets between wild type and klc4uw314 mutants.
source: We found no change in the percentage of retrograde comets between wild type and klc4uw314 mutants, suggesting KLC4 is not necessary for organization of MT polarity (Figure 9B and C).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 9B and C shows no significant difference in retrograde comet percentage.

claim: There is a significant increase in the frequency of anterograde EB3-GFP comets in peripheral axons, but not central axons, in klc4uw314 mutant RB neurons.
source: However, we found a significant increase in the frequency of anterograde comets in peripheral axons, but not central axons, in klc4uw314 mutant RB neurons (Figure 9B and D, Figure 9—figure supplement 1A), suggesting increased MT dynamics in peripheral axons.
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 9B and D demonstrates significantly increased comet frequency in mutant peripheral axons.

claim: The velocity of EB3-GFP comets, both anterograde and retrograde, is increased in peripheral and central axons in klc4uw314 mutants.
source: In addition, we found that the velocity of EB3-GFP comets, both anterograde and retrograde, was increased in peripheral and central axons in klc4uw314 mutants (Figure 9E, Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 9E and Figure 9—figure supplement 1B demonstrates increased comet velocity in mutants.

claim: There is no difference in the distance traveled by EB3-GFP comets between wild type and klc4uw314 mutants.
source: There was no difference in the distance traveled by EB3-GFP comets in any condition (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C,D), although duration of anterograde comet runs was reduced in peripheral axons, consistent with their increased velocity (Figure 9—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1C,D shows no significant difference in comet distance.

claim: Duration of anterograde EB3-GFP comet runs is reduced in peripheral axons in klc4uw314 mutants.
source: There was no difference in the distance traveled by EB3-GFP comets in any condition (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C,D), although duration of anterograde comet runs was reduced in peripheral axons, consistent with their increased velocity (Figure 9—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1E,F demonstrates reduced comet run duration in mutant peripheral axons.

claim: There is no difference in the frequency of EB3-GFP comets in nascent branches between wild type and klc4uw314 mutants.
source: We found no difference in the frequency of comets in nascent branches between wild type and mutants (Figure 10B).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 10B shows no significant difference in comet frequency in nascent branches.

claim: There is a significant reduction in the percentage of nascent branches with acetylated tubulin in klc4uw314 mutants.
source: We found a significant reduction in the percentage of nascent branches with acetylated tubulin in klc4uw314 mutants (Figure 10E).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 10E demonstrates significantly fewer nascent branches with acetylated tubulin in mutants.

claim: KLC4 is required for MTs to stabilize in newly formed branches.
source: This finding suggests that KLC4 is required for MTs to stabilize in newly formed branches.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation of reduced acetylated tubulin in nascent branches in mutants.

claim: klc4uw314 mutant larvae swim for a longer total time after touch stimulus than wild type larvae.
source: Klc4uw314 mutant larva swam for a longer total time (wild type median = 0.65 s, klc4uw314 1.49 s) and performed more swim bouts (wild type median = 1 bout, klc4uw314 mutants = 2 bouts) after touch stimulus than wild type larva (Figure 11B and C), suggesting KLC4 loss leads to hypersensitivity to touch.
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 11B demonstrates significantly longer swim response time in mutant larvae.

claim: klc4uw314 mutant larvae perform more swim bouts after touch stimulus than wild type larvae.
source: Klc4uw314 mutant larva swam for a longer total time (wild type median = 0.65 s, klc4uw314 1.49 s) and performed more swim bouts (wild type median = 1 bout, klc4uw314 mutants = 2 bouts) after touch stimulus than wild type larva (Figure 11B and C), suggesting KLC4 loss leads to hypersensitivity to touch.
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 11C demonstrates significantly more swim bouts in mutant larvae.

claim: KLC4 loss leads to hypersensitivity to touch.
source: Klc4uw314 mutant larva swam for a longer total time (wild type median = 0.65 s, klc4uw314 1.49 s) and performed more swim bouts (wild type median = 1 bout, klc4uw314 mutants = 2 bouts) after touch stimulus than wild type larva (Figure 11B and C), suggesting KLC4 loss leads to hypersensitivity to touch.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation of increased swim response in mutant larvae.

claim: klc4uw314 mutants are adult viable and fertile.
source: Indeed, we found that klc4uw314 mutants are adult viable and fertile but are smaller in size than their wild-type siblings (Figure 11—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript states that mutants survive to adulthood and can reproduce.

claim: klc4uw314 mutants are smaller in size than their wild-type siblings.
source: Indeed, we found that klc4uw314 mutants are adult viable and fertile but are smaller in size than their wild-type siblings (Figure 11—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Image shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1A demonstrates size difference between wild type and mutant adults.

claim: klc4uw314 mutants are on average 83.3% the size of their wild-type cousins at 7 weeks.
source: klc4uw314 mutants were on average 83.3% the size of their wild-type cousins at 7 weeks.
evidence: Body length measurements provide specific percentage of size difference.

claim: At 9 weeks, klc4uw314 mutant fish are measured at 84.6% the length of their wild-type cousins.
source: This difference remained at 9 weeks, despite both the wild type and klc4uw314 mutant fish increasing in size, with klc4uw314 mutant fish measured at 84.6% the length of their wild-type cousins.
evidence: Body length measurements provide specific percentage of size difference at 9 weeks.

claim: Wild type fish eat on average 90% of available zebrafish larvae in the feeding assay.
source: Wild type fish were effective feeders, eating on average 90% of available zebrafish larvae (Figure 11—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Feeding assay data shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1C provides specific percentage.

claim: klc4uw314 mutants eat on average only 60% of the larvae available in the feeding assay.
source: In comparison, klc4uw314 mutants ate on average only 60% of the larvae available.
evidence: Feeding assay data provides specific percentage for mutants.

claim: 90.9% of wild type fish explore the upper zone of the tank during the 3-min novel tank test, compared to only 18.8% of klc4uw314 mutant fish.
source: Analysis revealed that 90.9% of wild type fish explored the upper zone of the tank during the 3-min window, compared to only 18.8% of the klc4uw314 mutant fish (Figure 11E).
evidence: Novel tank test data shown in Figure 11E provides specific percentages.

claim: Wild type animals spend an average of 14 s in the upper region of the tank, compared to just 3.26 s for klc4uw314 mutants.
source: Wild type animals spent an average of 14 s in the upper region of the tank, compared to just 3.26 s for klc4uw314 mutants (Figure 11G).
evidence: Novel tank test data shown in Figure 11G provides specific time measurements.

claim: Freezing behavior is observed in an average of 43% of klc4uw314 mutant fish, and only 3% of wild type fish.
source: Notably, freezing behavior, defined for this experiment as cessation of all movement except for gills for at least 3 s, was observed in an average of 43% of mutant fish, and only 3% of wild type fish (Figure 11H).
evidence: Novel tank test data shown in Figure 11H provides specific percentages of fish exhibiting freezing behavior.

claim: 15.4% of klc4uw314 mutant fish, but no wild type animals, freeze for the full 3-min duration of the novel tank test.
source: 15.4% of klc4uw314 mutant fish, but no wild type animals, froze for the full 3-min duration of the experiment (Figure 11I).
evidence: Novel tank test data shown in Figure 11I provides specific percentages.

claim: Increased age improves freezing response of klc4uw314 mutants, with only 29.2% of aged individuals freezing during first 3 min of exposure to the novel tank.
source: We found that increased age improved freezing response of klc4uw314 mutants, with only 29.2% (8 out of a total of 23) of individuals tested freezing for more than 3 s during first 3 min of exposure to the novel tank (Figure 12A).
evidence: Habituation experiment data shown in Figure 12A provides specific percentages for aged fish.

claim: Upon subsequent exposures to the same tank, klc4uw314 mutant freezing behavior worsens, with 50% of mutants freezing by the sixth exposure.
source: Upon subsequent exposures to the same tank, klc4uw314 mutant freezing behavior worsened (Figure 12B, Figure 12—figure supplement 1A, B), with 50% of klc4uw314 mutants freezing by the sixth exposure, indicating that mutants fail to habituate freezing behavior.
evidence: Habituation experiment data shown in Figure 12B demonstrates worsening freezing behavior over multiple exposures.

claim: klc4uw314 mutants fail to habituate freezing behavior.
source: Upon subsequent exposures to the same tank, klc4uw314 mutant freezing behavior worsened (Figure 12B, Figure 12—figure supplement 1A, B), with 50% of klc4uw314 mutants freezing by the sixth exposure, indicating that mutants fail to habituate freezing behavior.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation that freezing behavior increases rather than decreases over multiple exposures.

claim: Both wild type and klc4uw314 mutants show habituation as measured by the percentage of time spent in the upper zone of the tank.
source: Interestingly, both wild type and klc4uw314 mutants did show habituation as measured by the percentage of time spent in the upper zone of the tank (Figure 12E).
evidence: Habituation experiment data shown in Figure 12E demonstrates increased time in upper zone over multiple exposures for both genotypes.

claim: The failure of klc4uw314 mutants to habituate freezing behavior is specific rather than reflecting a general deficit in habituation.
source: Thus, the failure of klc4uw314 mutants to habituate freezing behavior is specific rather than reflecting a general deficit in habituation.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation that mutants habituate exploration behavior but not freezing behavior.

claim: KLC4 has a specific function in patterning developing neurons rather than simply being required for general neuronal health.
source: Klc4 mutant neurons do not have a general growth defect, in that their axons grow faster than wild type axons. In addition, klc4 mutants are adult viable and show no signs of early neurodegeneration. These results suggest that KLC4 has a specific function in patterning developing neurons rather than simply being required for general neuronal health.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from observations that mutants have faster axon growth, are viable, and lack degeneration.

claim: The altered sensory arborization pattern in klc4 mutants affects sensory circuits.
source: Our finding that the mutant larvae are hypersensitive to touch stimuli suggests that the altered sensory arborization pattern affects sensory circuits.
evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the correlation between morphological defects and behavioral phenotype.

claim: Fasciculation of peripheral axons from neighboring neurons might lead to an increase in the number of neurons activated by a localized touch stimulus.
source: At least two axon defects could contribute to the increased response. Fasciculation of peripheral axons from neighboring neurons might lead to an increase in the number of neurons activated by a localized touch stimulus.
evidence: The mechanism is proposed based on the observed fasciculation phenotype and its potential functional consequences.

claim: The aberrant midline crossing of axons in klc4 mutants could cause inappropriate activation of contralateral neurons.
source: Also, the aberrant midline crossing of axons in mutants could cause inappropriate activation of contralateral neurons.
evidence: The mechanism is proposed based on the observed midline-crossing phenotype and its potential functional consequences.

claim: Adult klc4 mutants exhibit increased anxiety-like behavior.
source: Behavioral analysis also showed that klc4 mutant adults exhibit increased anxiety-like behavior, indicating roles for KLC4 in adult circuit function and identifying KLC4 as a novel gene associated with anxiety behavior.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from novel tank test results showing reduced exploration and increased freezing.

claim: KLC4 has roles in adult circuit function.
source: Behavioral analysis also showed that klc4 mutant adults exhibit increased anxiety-like behavior, indicating roles for KLC4 in adult circuit function and identifying KLC4 as a novel gene associated with anxiety behavior.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from behavioral deficits observed in adult mutants.

claim: KLC4 is a novel gene associated with anxiety behavior.
source: Behavioral analysis also showed that klc4 mutant adults exhibit increased anxiety-like behavior, indicating roles for KLC4 in adult circuit function and identifying KLC4 as a novel gene associated with anxiety behavior.
evidence: The manuscript identifies KLC4 as newly implicated in anxiety-like behavior based on the novel tank test results.

claim: Axon branching requires extensive cytoskeletal rearrangements.
source: Axon branching requires extensive cytoskeletal rearrangements (Kalil and Dent, 2014; Gallo, 2011; Winkle et al., 2016).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Branches begin as actin-based filopodial protrusions, which must be invaded by MTs to mature into branches.
source: Branches begin as actin-based filopodial protrusions, which must be invaded by MTs to mature into branches.
evidence: The statement describes established knowledge about branch formation mechanisms.

claim: MT severing by proteins such as katanin and spastin is required to facilitate MT invasion into branches.
source: MT severing by proteins such as katanin and spastin is required to facilitate invasion (Qiang et al., 2010; Yu et al., 1994; Yu et al., 2008) and branch points are hot spots of increased MT dynamics (Dent and Kalil, 2001).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Branch points are hot spots of increased MT dynamics.
source: MT severing by proteins such as katanin and spastin is required to facilitate invasion (Qiang et al., 2010; Yu et al., 1994; Yu et al., 2008) and branch points are hot spots of increased MT dynamics (Dent and Kalil, 2001).
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Kinesin-1 can bind MTs via the KHC C-terminal tail and crosslink or bundle MTs.
source: Kinesin-1 can bind MTs via the KHC C-terminal tail and crosslink or bundle MTs (Seeger and Rice, 2010; Navone et al., 1992).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Binding of KLC to KHC releases the autoinhibition of KHC and can tip the balance between kinesin-1's cargo transport activities and the ability of the KHC tail region to bind MTs.
source: Binding of KLC to KHC releases the autoinhibition of KHC and can tip the balance between kinesin-1's cargo transport activities and the ability of the KHC tail region to bind MTs (Wong and Rice, 2010; Cai et al., 2007; Chiba et al., 2021).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: KLC4 may promote the localized MT dynamics or severing that allows MTs to invade new branches, either by transporting/localizing MT regulators or by facilitating MT unbundling.
source: Our finding that MT dynamics are affected in klc4 mutants is consistent with a model in which KLC4 promotes the localized MT dynamics or severing that allows MTs to invade new branches, either by transporting/localizing MT regulators or by facilitating MT unbundling.
evidence: The model is proposed based on the observed MT dynamics defects in mutants.

claim: The increase in MT velocity in klc4 mutants could suggest an increase in MT sliding or altered regulation or localization of polymerization-promoting MAPs such as CRMP2.
source: The increase in MT velocity could suggest an increase in MT sliding or altered regulation or localization of polymerization-promoting MAPs such as CRMP2 (Nakamura et al., 2020).
evidence: The mechanism is proposed based on the observed increase in MT velocity and supported by citation.

claim: CRMP2 has been reported to influence MT polymerization and stabilization and has been found in complex with KLC4.
source: CRMP2 has been reported to influence MT polymerization and stabilization and has been found in complex with KLC4, supporting its potential role in KLC4-mediated effects on MTs (Liz et al., 2014; Koh et al., 2021).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: KLC4 may influence post-translational modifications of MTs and thereby affect stabilization of new branches.
source: MTs that invade nascent branches in klc4 mutants have less acetylation, suggesting KLC4 may influence post-translational modifications of MTs and thereby affect stabilization of new branches.
evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation of reduced acetylated tubulin in nascent branches in mutants.

claim: Regulated organelle/cargo transport and membrane remodeling are important for axon branching.

claim: A properly functioning endosomal trafficking system is necessary for RB axon branching.

evidence: The statement refers to prior work by the authors.

claim: KLC4 could potentially influence transport or localization of necessary organelle cargos, such as mitochondria or ER.

claim: KLC4 is the first motor protein shown to be involved in tiling.
source: Our results show that KLC4 is an important player in repulsion between sensory axons, and to our knowledge KLC4 is the first motor protein shown to be involved in tiling.

claim: DSCAM mediates sister branch separation in Drosophila mushroom body axons.

claim: The developmental phenotypes in klc4uw314 mutants appear to reflect problems with specific patterning of neuronal structure rather than problems in bulk cargo transport.

claim: The function of the KLC subunits of the kinesin-1 motor is to provide specificity to the process of localizing cargos to particular cell regions.
source: Thus our findings may reflect a general theme, that the function of the KLC subunits of the kinesin-1 motor are to provide specificity to the process of localizing cargos to particular cell regions.

claim: The human disease caused by KLC4 mutation may be caused by defects in developmental patterning.
source: Our results also give insight into mechanisms of the human disease caused by KLC4 mutation, which may be caused by defects in developmental patterning.

claim: Adult circuit function can be affected by both defects in circuit development and/or later defects in the function of neurons within circuits.
source: Adult circuit function can be affected by both defects in circuit development and/or later defects in the function of neurons within circuits.

claim: Zebrafish glucocorticoid receptor mutants show increased freezing and decreased exploratory behavior.

claim: RB neurons are traditionally thought to be a transient cell population that undergoes programmed cell death during larval stages.
source: RB neurons are traditionally thought to be a transient cell population that undergoes programmed cell death during larval stages.

claim: RB neurons have been shown to play significant roles in regulating larval behaviors.

claim: Hypersensitivity to touch is a common trait of autism spectrum disorder (ASD).

source: Interestingly, deletion of the ASD risk genes Mecp2 and Gabrb3 in mouse primary somatosensory neurons during development led to a reduction in exploratory behavior in the open-field test, while deletion of these genes only during adulthood caused no such impairment or anxiety behavior (Orefice et al., 2016).

evidence: The statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: klc4 is expressed in many cell types in the developing nervous system.
source: In addition to sensory neurons, klc4 is expressed in many cell types in the developing nervous system and thus likely has important roles in development and function of other neurons, which may include neurons that are directly involved in circuits mediating adult behavior.

claim: Kinesin-1 is a heterotetramer composed of homodimers of kinesin heavy chains (KHCs) and of kinesin light chains (KLCs).
source: Kinesin-1, the founding member of the kinesin superfamily of motor proteins, is a heterotetramer composed of homodimers of kinesin heavy chains (KHCs), which contain the MT binding and ATPase motor domains, and of kinesin light chains (KLCs), which interact with cargos.
evidence: The statement describes the established structure of kinesin-1.

claim: KHCs contain the MT binding and ATPase motor domains.
source: Kinesin-1, the founding member of the kinesin superfamily of motor proteins, is a heterotetramer composed of homodimers of kinesin heavy chains (KHCs), which contain the MT binding and ATPase motor domains, and of kinesin light chains (KLCs), which interact with cargos.
evidence: The statement describes the established functional domains of KHCs.

claim: KLCs interact with cargos.
source: Kinesin-1, the founding member of the kinesin superfamily of motor proteins, is a heterotetramer composed of homodimers of kinesin heavy chains (KHCs), which contain the MT binding and ATPase motor domains, and of kinesin light chains (KLCs), which interact with cargos.
evidence: The statement describes the established function of KLCs.

claim: Kinesin-1 can mediate long-distance, anterograde transport of multiple cargos including mitochondria, synaptic vesicle precursors, endosomes, lysosomes, and RNA granules.
source: Kinesin-1 can mediate long-distance, anterograde transport of multiple cargos including mitochondria, synaptic vesicle precursors, endosomes, lysosomes, and RNA granules (Hirokawa et al., 2010; Morfini et al., 2016).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Kinesin-1 has roles in organizing MT tracks.
source: Kinesin-1 also has roles in organizing MT tracks.

claim: Kinesin-1 is essential for proper development of the nervous system.
source: While it is clear that kinesin-1 is essential for proper development of the nervous system, the mechanisms by which it achieves cell-context specificity of its multiple functions and how its cargo-binding and MT-organizing functions are regulated have yet to be fully defined.
evidence: The statement presents established knowledge about kinesin-1's importance.

source: KLCs are known to mediate binding between the kinesin motor and cellular cargos, and also to activate the motor by releasing KHC autoinhibition (Morfini et al., 2016; Wong et al., 2010; Woźniak and Allan, 2006).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: KLCs activate the kinesin motor by releasing KHC autoinhibition.
source: KLCs are known to mediate binding between the kinesin motor and cellular cargos, and also to activate the motor by releasing KHC autoinhibition (Morfini et al., 2016; Wong et al., 2010; Woźniak and Allan, 2006).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Vertebrates have four klc genes (klc1-4), with klc1, 2 and 4 expressed in the nervous system.
source: Vertebrates have four klc genes (klc1-4), with klc1, 2 and 4 expressed in the nervous system, but our knowledge of the different roles played by individual KLCs in neurons remains very limited.
evidence: The statement presents established knowledge about klc genes.

source: In Drosophila, mutants for the single klc gene are lethal in larval stages and have defects in neural development (Gindhart et al., 1998; Mochizuki et al., 2011), indicating essential neural functions for KLC.
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: KLC1 and KLC2 have differing affinities for cargo adaptor proteins such as JIP1 and JIP3.

evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mouse klc1 mutants have functions for KLC1 in regulating motor behavior.
source: Studies of mouse klc1 mutants revealed functions for KLC1 in regulating motor behavior (Rahman et al., 1999), transport of amyloid precursor protein into axons (Kamal et al., 2000), phagosome transport in retinal pigment epithelium (Jiang et al., 2015), and axon guidance and cannabinoid recepter transport during neural development (Saez et al., 2020).

claim: Mouse klc2 mutants have hearing loss, cochlear hair cell loss and mislocalized mitochondria in hair cells.

claim: Peripheral and central axons have different capacity for branching.
source: Sensory neurons must extend separate axon branches to targets in the periphery and to the CNS to relay sensory information. Peripheral and central axons have different capacity for branching (Andersen et al., 2011), and behave differently when contacting other axons—central axons fasciculate with one another while peripheral axons show contact repulsion (Liu and Halloran, 2005; Sagasti et al., 2005).
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Central axons fasciculate with one another while peripheral axons show contact repulsion.
source: Sensory neurons must extend separate axon branches to targets in the periphery and to the CNS to relay sensory information. Peripheral and central axons have different capacity for branching (Andersen et al., 2011), and behave differently when contacting other axons—central axons fasciculate with one another while peripheral axons show contact repulsion (Liu and Halloran, 2005; Sagasti et al., 2005).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Contact repulsion of peripheral axons is necessary for establishment of proper axon arbor patterns that 'tile' with arbors from other neurons to effectively innervate the sensory field.
